thesis: Minecraft is not disposable content, but a system you can inhabit, play beyond its design, and redevelop through mods and servers.

volumes.payoffFan: Read the thesis first, then choose which volume to enter. This is not a walkthrough or changelog.
volumes.payoffDev: Every principle ships with non-transferable conditions. Do not start from Volume IV.
volumes.heading: How to Read This Book
volumes.thesis: The reading contract and route table. The two audiences need not read the same line — players come for "so that's why," developers for principles with their non-transferable conditions. You may skip around, but not past Volume II's first four chapters.

parts.title: Preface
parts.intent: Set the reader contract, forbid misreadings, and map the four volumes.

chapters.title: How to Read This Book
chapters.desc: The reading contract and route table. The two audiences need not read the same line — players come for "so that's why," developers for principles with their non-transferable conditions. You may skip around, but not past Volume II's first four chapters.
sections: Why the book starts from the voxel

chapters.title: The Thesis of This Book
chapters.desc: This book argues one sentence — Minecraft is not disposable content but a system you can inhabit, play beyond its design, and redevelop. Three volumes supply the evidence; the fourth is an exam.
sections: How the volumes divide the work
If you only have ten minutes

chapters.title: Method and Standards
chapters.desc: Why this book deserves trust: phenomena first, falsifiable claims, the two-editions rule, a ranking of sources, and an explicit list of what it will not cover. Method comes before opinions.
sections: What this book does not cover

volumes.payoffFan: Turn versions, mods, servers, and video into testable industrial history — not a nostalgia list.
volumes.payoffDev: What buy-once, UGC, dual engines, acquisition, and platformization each solved — and why “the next Minecraft” is so hard.
volumes.heading: Volume I · History and Business
volumes.thesis: How Minecraft grew from a 2009 prototype into a medium that communities, platforms, and capital kept redeveloping. Four parts: origins, becoming a culture, life after the acquisition, and a dissection of the business model. Not a changelog — a study of how choices grew into structure.

parts.title: Origins (2009–2011)
parts.intent: How a working prototype grew into a product on open development and a minimal loop.

chapters.title: From Infiniminer to Cave Game
chapters.desc: Infiniminer was abandoned and open-sourced less than a month after release; its "clone" became the best-selling game of all time. This chapter digs into the prehistory of destructible space — what Cave Game threw away, and how "unfinished" let it live as a product.
sections: Why "it copied Infiniminer" does not explain enough
Prehistory: destructible space already existed — always with a goal attached

chapters.title: Alpha: Developing in Public
chapters.desc: From Survival Test to Infdev, the world went from finite to infinite. The paid Alpha turned players into co-authors through weekly updates — and turned trust into a promise that had to be repaid continuously.
sections: Why anyone would pay for an unfinished game
Survival Test → Indev → Infdev: from finite to infinite
The feedback loop: forums, YouTube, word of mouth — not advertising
Early multiplayer: living in the same world as others
The paid Alpha: trust and lock-in happen together

chapters.title: Mojang, Beta, and the Release Version
chapters.desc: When a personal project becomes a studio, design authority moves from intuition to organization. Beta 1.8 was the first convergence toward a game; 1.0 completed a ceremony, not a system; and buy-once pricing set the ground note of every later revenue conflict.
sections: Did the game actually finish on release day?
Becoming a studio: roles, promises, MineCon
Beta 1.8: hunger, the Adventure Update, a split player base
The ethics of the price tag: buy once
Ceremony, not system: 1.0 did not end design

parts.title: Becoming a Culture (2011–2014)
parts.intent: How authors outside the base game defined in reverse what Minecraft is.

chapters.title: Mods as the Second Author
chapters.desc: Mods grew up alongside the game itself — Forge took the client seat, Bukkit the server, resource packs the skin. This chapter traces how the second authorship formed, and why Mojang absorbed the piston but left industry outside.
sections: "Vanilla Minecraft" was never a finished product
Three rivers: ModLoader/Forge, Bukkit, and resource packs
What industry, magic, and RPG mods filled in
Selective absorption: the piston gets in, industry does not
Credit and governance: should Mojang have managed mods?

chapters.title: The Server Is the New Game
chapters.desc: Players buy the client but play a different game living on a server. Creative, survival, and minigame servers are three societies on one engine; Hypixel and 2b2t are its two extremes — and the infrastructure beneath it all is more fragile than the game itself.
sections: You buy the client, you play the server
Players become operators: admins, economies, rules

chapters.title: Video, Education, and a Generation's Medium
chapters.desc: Let's Plays, tutorials, animations, and parody songs wrote Minecraft into the shared language of children and families, and Education Edition carried it into classrooms. Once "how to play" lives in video, what the base game should still teach becomes a late design question.
sections: Most people learned to play in videos
The genres: Let's Plays, tutorials, animations, song parodies
Children, families, and the safe creation seen by parents
Education Edition: the classroom sandbox rewrote whose game it is
What the base game still teaches: advancements and the recipe book as late make-up lessons

parts.title: After the Acquisition (2014–)
parts.intent: How capital, two product lines, and version politics turned protection into governance.

chapters.title: 微软收购
chapters.desc: 25 亿美元买下的是游戏、平台，还是一代人的入口。Notch 离场后，真正变量是分发、账号、合规与跨平台，不是「还能不能加方块」。
chapters.question: 这笔交易买下的到底是什么？
sections: 交易：结构、动机、时间线（可查）
Jeb 时代的风格转变（点到设计，不写人事）
产品线扩张：教育、Dungeons、Legends、电影——作为 IP 第二曲线的入口

chapters.title: Two Product Lines: Java and Bedrock
chapters.desc: From Pocket Edition to Bedrock, cross-platform was the product logic; feature divergence is brand debt. The Marketplace commercialized player creations and shut modding culture outside the gate. Two Minecrafts, not two skins.
sections: Why "buy one, play it all" does not work
PE to Bedrock: the cross-platform logic
The feature divergence table: redstone, combat, world format, modding capability
How accounts and distribution shape the design back

chapters.title: 版本政治与更新哲学
chapters.desc: 从「Notch 随手加」到主题版本。快照、实验玩法、数据包成为官方共创接口。洞穴与山崖证明生成系统可以当版本卖点。「原版纯度」是被更新不断改写的执念。
chapters.question: 官方如何与社区抢定义权？
sections: 为什么系统更深了，仍有人觉得「不是以前那个游戏」
共创接口：快照、实验玩法、数据包
主题版本：下界、洞穴与山崖
投票与失败实验：治理替代作者直觉

parts.title: Dissecting the Business Model
parts.intent: Revenue, grey economy, competition, and legacy on one map.

chapters.title: 收入结构
chapters.desc: 买断客户端之后，钱来自 Realms、Marketplace、IP 第二曲线、教育授权与区域发行。中国版证明同一品牌可以是不同合同。买断形象能维持，是因为变现被拆到周边层。
chapters.question: 钱从哪里来、不能从哪里来？
sections: 第二层：周边、电影、出版、主题公园

chapters.title: 模组、服务器与灰色经济
chapters.desc: 模组作者靠捐赠；服务器靠 Rank。盗版、第三方启动器、私人服务端与 Marketplace 并行。它同时是最开放、又最难被平台抽成的 UGC。Marketplace 卖商品，模组卖的是作者席。
chapters.question: 为何最开放又最难抽成？
sections: 免费模组养活了付费游戏
模组劳动：无偿、捐赠、打赏
灰色层作为生态事实（不教唆）
两种 UGC：Marketplace vs 模组

chapters.title: 竞争、模仿与产业影响
chapters.desc: Terraria、Vintage Story、Minetest、Hytale 是谱系对照。Roblox 才是真正的品类分叉：平台化对游戏化。「下一个 Minecraft」难，因为时机、工具链和一代人的入口不可复制。
chapters.question: 「下一个 Minecraft」为什么很难出现？
sections: Roblox：平台化 vs 游戏化
对开放世界、生存、沙盒、UGC 的具体影响

chapters.title: 作为文化遗产的 Minecraft
chapters.desc: 版本、存档、服务器和模组比引擎更难保存。当童年变成 IP，品牌管理、审查与创作自由开始摩擦。媒介一旦停止被再开发，就只剩 IP。
chapters.question: 谁来保存世界、模组与服务器？
sections: 一个旧模组世界现在还打得开吗
保存对象：版本、存档、服务器、模组
博物馆与研究（点到为止）
品牌、审查、家庭友好 vs 创作自由
卷一结语：卖的是可居住的媒介

volumes.payoffFan: See how a handful of rules combinatorially explode over a voxel world — the spine of the book.
volumes.payoffDev: Transferable principles with their premises spelled out; Volume II is the frozen layer everything else cites.
volumes.heading: Volume II · Game Design
volumes.thesis: Depth comes not from content volume but from the combinatorial explosion of a very few rules over a voxel world. Four parts: design primitives, how systems interlock, social design, and transferable principles. The book's spine is this volume.

parts.title: Design Primitives
parts.intent: The voxel, verbs, survival, and Creative mode — the frozen layer.

chapters.title: The Voxel as a Design Primitive
chapters.desc: The one-meter cube serves building, walking, fighting, and redstone at once because space is discrete, breakable, placeable, and countable. The world is the inventory; the voxel is not an art style — it is a system of measurement.
sections: Why "blocky game" is not an insult
Discrete space: trading precision for language
One system of measure across four ways to play
The comparison: what continuous-space sandboxes gain and lose

chapters.title: The Minimal Verb Set and Game Feel
chapters.desc: Look, walk, dig, place, craft, attack, use — seven verbs carry a whole game. This chapter explains why shipping without a build mode or a skill tree was the right call, and how tools amplify verbs instead of adding keys.
sections: Why modern sandboxes love an "editor mode"
Seven verbs, and the ones deliberately missing
The action lever: simple input, complex output

chapters.title: Survival as a Meaning Machine
chapters.desc: Hunger, night, and death are not a difficulty curve but rhythm devices: they hand out no goals, only moments that demand a response. The wood-stone-iron-diamond ladder is false progress, real teaching; home and safety are self-built; death drops, but does not destroy.
sections: With the monsters off, is it still Survival?
The resource ladder: false progress, real teaching
Death's restraint: it drops, but does not destroy
The world breathes: day-night and weather

chapters.title: Creative Mode Is Not a Level Editor
chapters.desc: Survival, Creative, Adventure, and Spectator are four permission configurations on one physics, not four games. Creative is parasitic on Survival's blocks, scale, and physics; infinite resources change the builder's social identity, not the world's rules.
sections: Why Creative still feels like playing Minecraft
What infinite resources change: social identity
The permission table: four modes, one spectrum
Comparison: Studio, GMod, and the real level editor

parts.title: How Systems Interlock
parts.intent: How crafting, worldgen, redstone, commands, mobs, and dimensions interlock.

chapters.title: Crafting, Items, and Inventory
chapters.desc: Depth is not added to the character but to things: grid crafting makes recipe knowledge a community dialect, items are portable slices of the world, and durability and enchanting build growth into objects. Anti-RPG was a choice, not an absence.
sections: How do you get "stronger" without a skill tree?
Grid crafting: spatial memory instead of a lookup menu
Items as slices of the world
Growth on things: durability, enchanting, smithing
Anti-RPG: a choice, not an absence

chapters.title: World Generation as Content Production
chapters.desc: Noise, biomes, and structures each mind one layer, and what they produce is not content but difference; the seed is infinity's rhetoric, the Far Lands its crack, and "not finding" is exploration's fuel. The design contract of procedural content is explorable, not completable.
sections: Why the same mountains can be looked at for a lifetime
The division of labor: noise, biomes, structures
The rhetoric of infinity: seeds, the Far Lands, the border
Generation as the selling point: what Caves & Cliffs proves

chapters.title: Redstone: Physics as Programming
chapters.desc: The electricity metaphor failed, yet logic circuits grew out of the wreckage. The game teaches nothing, so the community wrote the textbook; gates, clocks, flying machines, and computers are computation invented by players. This chapter erects the "misusable system": designers deliver physics, not a play list.
sections: Redstone on the Wiki and "redstone" in the game are not the same thing
It is not electricity: why the metaphor failed
Invented computation: gates, clocks, flying machines, computers
Three ways to be programmable: mechanism / circuit / script — which one Minecraft chose

chapters.title: Commands, Datapacks, and Maps
chapters.desc: The command block turns the operator into the level designer, and the datapack is the officially sanctioned data-driven mod. Four map genres parasitize one and the same physics — and where data-driven design meets its limit is exactly where mods begin.
sections: The command block: the operator becomes the level designer
Type parasitism: how map genres ride one physics
The limits: when you must write a new system

chapters.title: Mobs, Combat, and Threats
chapters.desc: Mobs are rhythm devices and a movement tax, not the main act of content; bosses stay few and each holds one job; PvP is an arena the community invented. Combat was deliberately kept at "good enough," ceding depth to building and survival.
sections: Why the attack cooldown tore the community apart
Rhythm devices: night, creepers, and the undead
Boss restraint: the dragon, the wither, and the warden hold different jobs
PvP is an arena the community invented
Why it cannot be an action game

chapters.title: Dimensions, Advancements, and the Endgame
chapters.desc: The Nether and the End are rule variants, not levels; advancements are suggestions, not quests; the official late game ships levers, not endpoints. The real endgame is player-built — a game with no ending stays alive on voluntary goals that regenerate.
sections: The official late game: villagers, beacons, and elytra
The players' late game: ice roads, factories, and server civilizations

parts.title: Social Design
parts.intent: Multiplayer defaults, who makes rules, mods as design method.

chapters.title: Multiplayer Is the Default
chapters.desc: Singleplayer worlds are full of design prepared for others — doors, beds, chests, signs. LAN, Realms, and public servers are three social radii; seeds, mods, and video reconnect a singleplayer save to society, with delay. Multiplayer is the default state, not an add-on mode.
sections: Why the singleplayer world is full of social metaphors
Grief, trust, and territory: the politics of an open world
Delayed multiplayer: seeds, mods, and video

chapters.title: 规则由谁制定
chapters.desc: 游戏规则、难度、命令权限是引擎立法。插件是服务器立法。不成文宪法是不破坏、不作弊、审美共识。2b2t 是无规则的极限实验。设计师不只坐在 Mojang。
chapters.question: 谁才是真正的设计师？
sections: 关掉怪物掉落之后，还是不是同一款游戏

chapters.title: 模组作为设计方法
chapters.desc: 加系统与加内容是模组成功的两种模式。整合包是策展即设计。工业 / 魔法 / RPG 在补结构空洞。正作收编应增加动词或可误用物理，而不是增加内容包。
chapters.question: 正作该吸收什么、不该吸收什么？

chapters.title: 留白、涌现与玩家作者性
chapters.desc: 目标外包：游戏提供动词，玩家提供叙事。涌现是约束下的必然，不是意外。玩具 vs 游戏之争在此被终结。建造、红石、地图、影像是同一作者权利。
chapters.question: 涌现是意外还是必然？
sections: 「我不知道这游戏要干什么」为何可以是好评
涌现 = 约束下的必然
对照：《旷野之息》《动物森友会》《Dwarf Fortress》——各说明「不像」的那一点
同一权利：建造 / 红石 / 地图 / 影像

chapters.title: 约束即深度
chapters.desc: 不真实的物理（重力例外、水与岩浆）往往更好玩。现代化更新的风险是填满留白。特例方块可能是深度也可能是债。停手原则：新系统必须增加动词，而不是增加菜单。

chapters.title: 可迁移原则清单
chapters.desc: 十二条可带走原则，加上不可复制条件，加上 Minecraft-like 反面教材。卷二收束：能住进去的系统，不是通关即弃的内容。
chapters.question: 开发者到底能拿走什么？
sections: 为什么 Minecraft-like 总是「像但不长」
十二条原则（必须用这十二条，可改表述不可换核）：
最小动词，深度来自组合
程序内容合同 = 可探索
约束即深度；不真实可以更好玩
模式是权限，不是四个游戏
社会契约是设计的一半
模组 / 数据驱动是第一公民
新系统必须增加动词，不增加菜单
不可复制条件：时机、媒介窗口、二十年工具链、未定义行为被收编为 API
反面教材：至少三种「抄了皮、丢了骨」的机制类型

volumes.payoffFan: Follow a working prototype dragged into impossible scale — architecture debt and design freedom share one origin.
volumes.payoffDev: Which debts are assets, which are real constraints, and why the moddable engine is the complete product.
volumes.heading: Volume III · Technical Implementation

parts.intent: Mods, datapacks, Java runtime, Bedrock, and servers.

chapters.title: 模组与插件架构
chapters.desc: 字节码、Mixin、Forge / Fabric / NeoForge。Bukkit / Paper 是另一条河。没有稳定 API 时，注入即 API，升级变成政治。兼容矩阵：版本 × 加载器 × 模组。模组比引擎更难维护。
chapters.question: 为什么模组比引擎更难维护？
sections: 为什么每个大版本都是模组的末日

chapters.title: 数据包、资源包与数据驱动
chapters.desc: 扁平化之后的命名空间世界。数据包能改什么、不能改什么。资源包与数据分工。官方扩展面故意停在「新动词」之前。数据驱动是温和模组的政治。
chapters.question: 官方扩展面的边界在哪？
sections: 为什么有了数据包还是要写 Java
能做 / 必须写代码 对照表

chapters.title: Java 版运行时
chapters.desc: 2009 年选 Java 证明了可移植与模组性，也卡住了性能与发布。GC、JIT、启动器、版本隔离。性能史从「能跑」到各类优化模组。语言是历史偶然，不是设计本质。
chapters.question: Java 证明了什么、卡住了什么？

chapters.title: Bedrock 作为另一次实现
chapters.desc: C++、跨平台、独立渲染栈。行为包、附加包、脚本 API。红石 / 战斗 / 世界格式的语义分叉比性能差异更致命。Marketplace 技术反过来塑造能做什么。换语言重写之后，分叉会变成两个游戏。
chapters.question: 语义差异为何比性能差异更致命？

chapters.title: 服务端与规模
chapters.desc: 原版服务端、Paper、分片实验。视距 vs 模拟距离。代理、群组、反作弊、备份。万人网络已经是另一种引擎用法。原版没有把兴趣管理当成一等公民。
chapters.question: 同一内核如何同时服务单人档与万人网络？
sections: 单人档和万人服真的是同一个程序吗
运维栈：代理、反作弊、回滚
大型服务器作为另一种引擎用法

parts.title: Engineering Lessons
parts.intent: Technical debt and the moddable engine as complete product.

chapters.title: Technical Debt as Product Strategy
chapters.desc: "Release first, fix later" held in Minecraft only because four external conditions held at once — growth masking the debt, cash flow buying the windows, the community carrying the debt, compatibility locking the semantics. The account of the refactoring windows, the tacit terms of the folk official implementations, and the parts of the myth ordinary projects cannot reuse.
sections: The myth of "if it runs, sell it"
The refactoring windows: loans bought with trust
What the indie developer cannot copy
Folk official implementations: the socialized repayment of debt

chapters.title: An Engine That Can Be Modded Is the Complete Product
chapters.desc: Volume III's close: kernel, protocol, data plane, toolchain, and community implementations form one inseparable composite product; which debts are in fact assets; and the five-item minimal kernel — the first answer sheet for the rewrite exam.
sections: A Minecraft that cannot be redeveloped is only a client
Measured against Volume II: how implementation illuminates design

volumes.payoffFan: An exam, not a work order: what is essence, what is historical accident.
volumes.payoffDev: Compatibility as ethics toward player time; who may rewrite; the checklist before any greenfield project.
volumes.heading: Volume IV · The Rewrite
volumes.thesis: If it were rewritten today, which essentials must be kept and which accidents can be peeled away — an exam, not a work order. Three parts: defining the problem, an architecture proposal, product and ethics. Read Volume II chapter 16 and Volume III chapter 18 before entering.

parts.title: Defining the Problem Before Rewriting
parts.intent: Four products that cannot substitute for one another; invariants and accidents.

chapters.title: What Exactly Are We Rewriting
chapters.desc: "Rewrite Minecraft" packs at least four undertakings that cannot substitute for one another. This chapter separates the vanilla experience, the mod platform, the server platform, and the creation tools; draws the line between the compatibility road and the inheritance road; and declares that this volume sets exam questions, not answers.
sections: First, a ban on "doing Minecraft again"
This volume is the exam, not the work order

chapters.title: Design Invariants That Must Be Kept
chapters.desc: The one-meter grid, the breakable world, the minimal verb set, outsourced goals, misusable physics, a world that outlives the engine, redevelopment as a first-class citizen — seven invariants examined one by one, each with its degradation scenario and its criterion for being falsified.
sections: Which part of the "Minecraft feel" is rules
Seven invariants, examined one by one

chapters.title: Discardable Accidents
chapters.desc: The Java runtime, the one global 20-TPS clock, the dual-edition split, the semantic freeze on parts of the implementation — every one of these accidents can be discarded, but each must first prove that the invariant it hosted has somewhere new to live.
sections: The language runtime: discard Java, re-house portability and reversibility
The one global clock: discard the unified 20-TPS beat, re-house causal discipline
The dual-edition split: discard the second implementation, re-house cross-platform and the business model
The semantic freeze on implementation details: discard the "quirks", pay off the dependence first

parts.title: Architecture Proposal
parts.intent: World representation, scheduling, scripting, network, rendering.

chapters.title: World Representation
chapters.desc: Sparse voxels, componentized state, the world as an object, deterministic replay, old saves as first-class citizens — the rewritten world representation must serve, at once, one big world housing tens of thousands and tens of thousands of small worlds each their own.
sections: Sparsity and palettes: making emptiness free
State and components: moving behavior onto the data plane too
The world as an object: from the process's fate to operations on data
Deterministic replay: making the past computable too
Old saves: first-class citizenship is not a slogan

chapters.title: Simulation Scheduling
chapters.desc: Interest as a first-class citizen, causality-tiered settlement, explicit entity budgets, reproducible time travel — a scheduling design in which singleplayer and ten-thousand-player servers share one kernel, and how redstone causality keeps from being torn apart.
sections: The limits of the global 20 TPS
Interest management and sharding: the first step of explicitness
Causal tiers: redstone, fluids, and entities each in their place
Entity budgets and LOD: writing the tax into the institution
Time-travel debugging: causal explainability's final form
Redstone causality, unshattered: the acceptance test

chapters.title: The Two Layers of Scripts and Mods
chapters.desc: The sandbox layer and the native layer each fail alone — two single-layer designs and the exact ways they die, the separation of blast radii, three lines of stable API, hot reload and versioned schemas, and author experience as a formal part of the product.
sections: The failure modes of all-script and all-native
The two-layer model and the separation of blast radii
The stable API surface: three lines
Hot reload and schemas: author productivity is ecosystem productivity

chapters.title: Networking, Permissions, and the Sinking of Social Functions
chapters.desc: Land claims, backups, rollbacks, replay arbitration, permission tiers — the "standard legal code" every server owner legislates over and over should sink into the engine as first-class functions; ownership becomes a first-class concept, anticheat becomes system structure, and the four modes generalize into a continuous permission matrix.
sections: Every server owner rewrites the same law
Sinking the social checklist: primitives, not a platform
Generalizing the permission model: from four notches to one matrix

chapters.title: Rendering and Authoring Tools
chapters.desc: The hand-feel is still the product, and rendering debt should be cleared natively along directions the community has already validated; structure editing, function debugging, and data inspection should be built in as the author seat's basic infrastructure — and tools and runtime must share one world model.
sections: The hand-feel is still the product
Four rendering principles, not a shopping guide
Built-in tools: the author seat's infrastructure, nationalized
From resource packs to the asset graph
Tools and runtime: one world model

parts.title: Product and Ethics
parts.intent: Compatibility ethics, who may rewrite, seeing the original clearly.

chapters.title: The Compatibility Strategy
chapters.desc: Old saves and the old ecosystem are the rewrite's ticket of admission: this chapter argues why reading old saves is an obligation rather than a feature, lays out three channels for reading them and the two-path plan for redstone, and shows how namespace discipline and the costs of compatibility get written into the product's scope.
sections: Player time lives in the save
Redstone's two paths: the simulation layer and the new semantics

chapters.title: Who Holds the Right to Rewrite
chapters.desc: Protocol, assets, and brand are habitually conflated. This chapter takes the three apart, inventories what community projects, the officials, and open source can each promise — and are fated never to promise — and swaps the acceptance standard from "more alike" back to "the invariants still hold."
sections: Three things that must not be conflated
What the three subjects can promise
The different needs of three kinds of users
The acceptance standard: the invariants still hold

chapters.title: Rewriting to See the Original Clearly
chapters.desc: The book's closing word: the finalized list of essential properties, the three verb claims collected and one amendment confessed; and an answer to the most important question — if no one ever rewrites, why this volume was still worth writing.
sections: Back to the opening thesis: accepting the three claims
If no one ever rewrites, why it is still worth writing
The book's closing word: three verbs

volumes.payoffFan: Timeline and glossary for lookup — not for argument.
volumes.payoffDev: Comparison tables and exercises. No reference implementations.
volumes.heading: Appendix

parts.title: Reference
parts.intent: Timeline, people, comparisons, glossary, sources, and exercises — for lookup, not argument.

chapters.title: Timeline
chapters.desc: Product, community, and business events from 2009 to 2026, compared year by year across three parallel tracks. Events only; every entry follows items verifiable on Minecraft Wiki and Wikipedia.

chapters.title: People and Organizations
chapters.desc: A quick reference to the people and organizations that appear in the main edition: three to six lines each, with their role and links into the chapters. For looking things up, not for passing judgment.

chapters.title: Java and Bedrock Compared
chapters.desc: An item-by-item comparison of the two product lines across four layers: gameplay rules, data formats, the extension ecosystem, and business and platform. Each row links to the full argument in the main edition.

chapters.title: Glossary
chapters.desc: A quick reference to the book's high-frequency terms, one sentence per word. Five groups — world and data, time and simulation, extension and ecosystem, editions and products, community and analysis — plus a handful of concepts coined by this book. The definition is all there is; for the arguments, see the main volumes.
sections: Community and analysis (including this book's concepts)

chapters.title: Sources and References
chapters.desc: The main sources used in the main volumes, sorted by credibility tier: official material, wiki and community documentation, news and industry coverage, archives and primary documents. For checking against, not for arguing.

chapters.title: Developer Exercises
chapters.desc: Eight hands-on exercises: a minimal voxel sandbox, a misusable system, a save migrator, a redstone semantics test suite, an interest-driven scheduler, a two-layer extension, a permission matrix, and event-sourcing replay. Each gives a goal, constraints, source chapters, and a passing standard — never an implementation.
sections: IV. A Redstone Semantics Test Suite
